title: Connection-consistent mesh sharding and tiered load-shedding for active-active API failover
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Goal: Implement an active-active gateway strategy that preserves in-flight streaming/connection continuity while enabling controlled traffic shifts between regions. We will adopt a mesh sharding approach that prefers connection-consistent routing (per-connection or per-session sticky assignment) with fast reconfiguration and tiered load-shedding hooks to protect SLOs and service health.

Scope: gateway and edge routing layer, session routing rules, regional circuit-breakers, hierarchical load-shedding policy (gateway-level soft degrade, edge reject, model-variant fallback), telemetry + SLO enforcement. This ticket covers design and a first-pass implementation of the routing table, sharding algorithm, and load-shedding policy; follow-ups will implement autoscaling integration and Dedicated-specific configs.

Background & constraints: Redwood supports streaming API sessions where clients maintain long-lived websockets or chunked HTTP streams carrying per-session KV state (prefix caches). Blindly moving a stream between regions causes token/kv desync and user-visible truncation. Our existing simple region-fallback causes replay/duplication and increased tail latency. Constraints include: minimal added per-request latency at the gateway, eventual consistency of shard-state across border routers, preserving p50/p95 latency targets, and avoiding cross-region KV fetches that amplify cost.

Proposed approach (summary):
- Consistent mesh sharding: assign connection/session to a logical shard using a sticky key (connection id or session cookie) and consistent hashing ring; shards are mapped to a preferred region/node pool.
- Fast local reconfiguration: per-edge route table holds shard->endpoint mapping with TTL and sequence versioning; updates use compact change sets propagated via gossip within a region and push to paired regions.
- Streaming continuity: for active streaming sessions, allow in-region sticky servicing and only migrate sessions when a graceful handoff is negotiated (explicit transfer token exchanged) or when forced by health/capacity triggers.
- Tiered load-shedding: implement three levels: 1) soft degrade (lower model size, reduce max tokens, or batch more aggressively), 2) session shed (pause/queue new streams with backpressure headers), 3) hard reject (HTTP 503) with structured Retry-After and fallback to a lower-tier model.
- Region circuit-breakers: track error rates, tail latency, and saturation per-region+model; open breaker when error budget threshold crossed. Breaker state machine enforces traffic dampening and prevents cascading failures.

Key metrics/SLOs addressed: keep hosted API p95 latency for interactive streams under configured SLO (example: p95 < 350ms) by shedding lower-priority traffic and routing to warm-capacity pools; preserve error budget burn rate below configured threshold during failovers; measure continuity (percentage of streams that complete without requiring client reconnect).
acceptance_criteria: Routing invariants: given a connection id and current route table, 99.9% of requests routed to the same shard mapping for 24h unless an update is applied
Graceful streaming handoff: instrumented path that migrates an active stream to another region with less than 250ms client-perceived interruption in 90% of test cases (lab simulation)
Tiered shedding works end-to-end: soft degrade, session shed, and hard reject are triggerable by policy and observable via dashboard metrics and logs
Circuit-breaker correctness: simulated region failure causes traffic to be dampened and redirected according to policy without violating p99 latency SLO for remaining healthy traffic
Canary rollout: feature flag gate with 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% ramps and automated rollback if SLO guard rails breach during the canary
Docs & runbook: design doc and oncall runbook created with clear remediation steps for migration and rollback
implementation_notes: Sharding: use Rendezvous (highest-random-weight) hashing for even distribution and minimal remapping when nodes change
Route table: compact versioned delta updates (v2) over existing pubsub; avoid large full-table pushes to edges
State: keep only ephemeral sticky mappings at gateways; authoritative mapping lives in control plane cache to avoid cross-region KV fetches on hot path
Streaming handoff: implement handshake token that encapsulates last-known KV sequence and offset; receiving region validates token and rehydrates prefix cache from snapshot store asynchronously

Load-shedding policy: expressable in DSL with priority buckets (interactive, background, internal); gateways evaluate policy before admission and return structured problem details for backoff guidance
Circuit-breakers: two-level breakers (region-level and per-model-instance); breakers expose reason codes for observability and automated escalation
rollout_plan: Unit + integration tests in CI simulating cross-region latency and region partition
Internal dogfood in staging with synthetic traffic that mirrors customer streaming mixes
1% production canary routed from a single edge cluster; monitor latency, error budget burn, continuity metric for 24h
If healthy, ramp to 5% then 25% each with 24h windows and automated SLO gates; full roll when stable
Post-rollout: run 72h chaos experiment (node drains, region load spike) and capture metrics for postmortem
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: cross-region KV rehydration latency may cause poor handoff experience. Mitigation: rely on snapshot+lazy-rehydrate and prefer in-region servicing until warm copies available.

Risk: inconsistent route-table state leads to split-brain routing. Mitigation: use sequence numbers, TTLs, and conservative traffic-shifting heuristics; require manual approval for mass-shift operations.

Risk: misclassification of traffic priority causing customer-visible rejects. Mitigation: start with internal-only priority buckets and require opt-in for customer workloads; expose metrics and sample traces for tuning.
Risk: complexity of DSL and policies. Mitigation: ship small set of composable primitives and pre-built safe policies; move to richer DSL only after stable usage patterns observed.
